title: Beyond Billing: The Full Potential of Cellular AMI | Badger Meter
summary: AMI systems can be connected to network sensors and instruments, creating a level of visibility into and control over water distribution systems that simply isn’t possible with flow data alone.
body_text: One of the many advantages of cellular advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) systems is that they enable water utilities to get accurate usage data from anywhere in the field or office. For water utilities looking to transition away from labor-intensive manual meter reading or the one-dimensional data collected from drive-by automated meter reading (AMR) , cellular AMI is a logical step. While some water utilities may struggle to justify an investment into cellular AMI or view it only as a solution to meter reads and billing, the capabilities of these systems extend far beyond that. As battery and communication technology evolves, AMI systems can be connected to network sensors and instruments, creating a level of visibility into and control over water distribution systems that simply isn’t possible with flow data alone. Supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems are essential tools for automating and optimizing specific treatment plant processes. Cellular AMI systems enhance those capabilities, supplementing traditional SCADA systems with flow data across a network. The near real-time data serves as an indicator of demand changes across distributed data collection points. This level of insight can help to increase responsiveness and, for budget-conscious water utilities, generate a better return on investment (ROI) for an AMI system—especially when the flow data is leveraged for additional data integration applications. Pressure-Driven Precision Pressure sensors are integral to understanding a water system’s operational parameters. While flow meters provide insights into water movement, pressure sensors offer valuable information about how a system is responding to operating changes and demand fluctuations. Monitoring pressure at a high resolution can be useful for helping operators identify potential trouble spots or areas requiring further investigation. Although some flow meters also have pressure and temperature measurement capabilities, the deployment of additional pressure sensors in the network enables utilities to examine specific incidents like water hammer events and pressure surges. Deeper insights provide operators with context to identify root causes, demonstrating how the synergy between pressure and flow data enables proactive maintenance strategies. Maintaining service pressure is another key function of pressure sensors. By deploying these sensors strategically throughout the network, utilities gain invaluable insights into actual pressure conditions experienced by end customers around the clock and throughout the year. This real-time data allows utilities to adjust pressure levels dynamically. This can optimize network operations to meet service standards and, due to added efficiency, reduce pumping costs and electricity consumption. Water Quality Assurance The top three expenses impacting water utilities are power, personnel, and chemical costs—and water quality management affects all three. As water moves through the system, its quality is dynamic and constantly changing. The integration of real-time water quality monitoring in AMI systems provides utilities with a steady stream of data points that operators can use to swiftly identify fluctuations and trends, especially in areas with varying demand or for critical customers like hospitals and dialysis centers. Today’s water quality monitoring systems track more than just pH and chlorine levels; they measure a broad spectrum of substances and conditions that influence water chemistry. Unlike periodic sampling, real-time water quality data eliminates guesswork, empowering water utilities with actionable insights to detect water quality issues as they happen. This proactive approach enables utilities to make operational adjustments promptly, optimizing treatment processes and streamlining resource allocation. Data-Driven Efficiency For years, SCADA and water network data management tools have provided dashboards with a comprehensive view of system operations, ranging from high-level management insights to detailed technical data. With many systems now operating in the cloud , utilities have more flexibility to access and utilize data points according to their specific needs. Centralized data systems offer utilities the advantage of accessing a unified repository that presents data consistently and allows for multidimensional analysis. This capability enables utilities to detect trends, identify patterns, and make informed decisions regarding system maintenance, customer service, and operational efficiency. Furthermore, transparent and accessible data fosters collaboration and information sharing across stakeholders for efficient resource allocation and improved service delivery. Choosing an AMI System When choosing an AMI system, water utilities should consider the following factors: Needs of the utility. The system must be able to address specific pain points. Vendor experience. This refers both to the number of years the company has been in business as well as the background of the staff. For example, someone who has actually worked for (not just with) a utility is more likely to understand which features or systems can provide the desired solution without over- or underselling. Associated costs. Reduced truck rolls and more accurate bills are some of the obvious benefits of AMI for billing and meter reads. But with a full system AMI that includes pressure sensors and water quality monitoring, utilities can realize much bigger returns by reducing chemical costs, identifying and fixing leaks faster (and with less manpower), and more. There are also less tangible ROIs, such as faster customer service resolutions, fewer complaints, and more consistent water quality. The impact of cellular AMI systems on water utility operations can be truly transformational, delivering benefits far beyond meter reads and billing. With the ability to integrate data from pressure sensors and real-time water quality monitoring, AMI systems bring measurable value to water utilities by ensuring better visibility and control over the entire distribution system. By leveraging a centralized data system, AMI equips water utilities with the insights they need to improve system efficiency, reduce expenses and deliver excellent customer service to their communities.

title: Guía completa sobre las jeringas de anestesia dental
summary: Conoce las características y aspectos importantes a considerar para escoger las jeringas dentales adecuadas con esta guía completa.
body_text: Las jeringas de anestesia dental son uno de los implementos más utilizados para realizar procedimientos en odontología. Su uso es esencial para garantizar la comodidad del paciente, asegurando que se puedan completar los tratamientos de manera satisfactoria. Quédate para saber qué tipo de jeringas escoger para tu clínica dental. ¿Cuál es la función de las jeringas de anestesia dental? En odontología, se requiere de un alto nivel de precisión para completar algunos tratamientos, es por ello que es fundamental que el paciente no sienta dolor o molestia durante la ejecución del proceso. Es aquí donde entra la anestesia dental para garantizar que los procedimientos sean indoloros. La anestesia, es administrada a través de jeringas dentales, una herramienta indispensable con un diseño ergonómico y con la precisión necesaria para asegurar la comodidad del paciente y la efectividad del tratamiento. ¿Cuáles son las partes de una jeringa de anestesia dental? Las jeringas de anestesia de uso odontológico están compuestas por 4 partes básicas. Cuerpo: parte cilíndrica donde va el tubo de anestesia. Punta enroscada: zona inferior de la jeringa donde se encaja la aguja. Zona de sujeción: es la parte superior donde se apoyan los dedos para empujar el émbolo. Suele tener forma de anillo o de T. Pistón o émbolo: pieza que se une y se engancha a la tapa de goma del tubo de anestesia. Estas son las partes que componen la herramienta principal para llevar a cabo procedimientos dentales, permitiendo la correcta infiltración de la anestesia. Tipos de jeringas de anestesia dental Existen diferentes tipos de jeringas de anestesia dental comúnmente empleadas en las clínicas dentales. Entre ellas están: Jeringas carpule Están hechas de acero inoxidable. Son diseñadas para administrar la anestesia a través de carpules prellenados que no son recargables y requieren ser esterilizadas en autoclave . Este tipo de jeringas garantizan una dosificación precisa y un flujo suave del anestésico. Su diseño ergonómico permite un manejo cómodo y una fácil aspiración del líquido. Jeringas desechables Estas jeringas son fabricadas en plástico, por lo que eliminan la necesidad de esterilización después de cada uso, lo que ahorra tiempo y garantiza la higiene, sin embargo, no son tan resistentes. Su diseño de un solo uso reduce el riesgo de contaminación cruzada y garantiza la seguridad del paciente. Pero suelen tener un diseño que puede resultar incómodo al momento de la aplicación. Jeringas recargables Son diseñadas de materiales como el acero inoxidable o aleaciones. Pueden usarse con diferentes tipos de cartuchos y permiten ser esterilizadas mediante varios métodos. Este tipo de jeringa tiene la particularidad de que pueden ser recargadas manualmente con anestesia líquida. Jeringas de presión Proporciona una aplicación rápida y sencilla de la anestesia, permitiendo la dosificación exacta de la misma, minimizando el riesgo de sobredosis o subdosis. Este tipo de jeringas son especialmente usadas para romper la resistencia tisular. Jeringas articuladas Estas jeringas permiten insertar cartuchos de anestesia local fácilmente. Su mecanismo simplificado asegura una aspiración efectiva. Son de uso sencillo y ofrecen un control preciso durante la inyección. No obstante, su uso correcto exige mayor preparación y práctica, ya que la precisión en la dosificación depende de la habilidad del dentista. Jeringas eléctricas Facilitan una mayor precisión, velocidad y control del flujo de anestesia al momento de la aplicación. Lo cual disminuye la incomodidad del paciente durante el proceso. Debido a su diseño compacto y su facilidad de uso, la jeringa eléctrica es ideal para procedimientos en zonas de difícil acceso, como la parte posterior de la boca o alrededor de nervios. ¿Qué tener en cuenta para elegir el tipo de jeringas más conveniente para tu consultorio? Al ser un instrumento central para la aplicación de procedimientos dentales, es pertinente conocer las características más importantes a tener en cuenta al momento de escoger el tipo de jeringa que se utilizara en tu consultorio. Entre los aspectos a tomar en cuenta están: Material de fabricación : seleccionar materiales de alta calidad que sean duraderos, fáciles de limpiar y que soporten procesos de esterilización constantes sin deteriorarse. Precisión y control : que facilite una dosificación precisa y un control del flujo de anestésico con el émbolo para garantizar una administración adecuada y cómoda para el paciente. Compatibilidad con agujas dentales de diferentes fabricantes : utilizadas comúnmente en la práctica odontológica, permitiendo mayor versatilidad y reutilización. Peso de acuerdo a su uso : que sea posible su manipulación con una sola mano. ¿Cómo gestionar la aplicación de la anestesia dental? Los aspectos que motivan a los pacientes a volver una y otra vez a la consulta odontológica son aquellos que hacen que la experiencia de asistir a la clínica dental sea más fácil y amena, desde pedir el turno de manera sencilla hasta no sentir dolor durante la realización del tratamiento (ya sea endodoncia, ortodoncia, entre otros). En cuanto a los procedimientos odontológicos indoloros, los odontólogos suelen emplear técnicas de anestesia dental infiltrativa , la cual es aplicada directamente alrededor de terminaciones nerviosas mediante el uso de jeringas especializadas para que la infiltración sea lo menos doloroso posible. Es por esto que, conocer y utilizar las jeringas de anestesia adecuadas es un factor crucial para evitar la interrupción prematura, el retraso del tratamiento odontológico o dolores innecesarios al paciente. Las jeringas de anestesia dentales son herramientas esenciales para garantizar la comodidad y seguridad de los pacientes durante los tratamientos. Las innovaciones en el diseño y la técnica de administración continúan mejorando la experiencia tanto para los pacientes como para los profesionales. title: Belden’s DuetConnect Hybrid Termination Box Brings Fiber and Copper Together While Protecting Against Damage
summary: Hybrid cable termination is made easier, cleaner and more efficient while also maintaining a separation between copper and fiber
body_text: St. Louis, Missouri – May 29, 2024 – Belden Inc. (NYSE: BDC), a leading global supplier of network infrastructure and digitization solutions, is excited to announce the launch of its new DuetConnect Hybrid Termination Box, which allows installers to properly terminate fiber and copper in the same box while safeguarding against damage. As the demand for downloading and uploading capabilities, clear streaming and immersive experiences are on the rise, fiber infrastructure deployments allow consumers to confidently use online devices without downtime or delays. Many IoT devices that support these connections, including cameras, optical network terminals (ONTs) and distributed antenna systems (DAS), are being deployed in locations where local power is vital—but isn’t always available or accessible. Installers often support these installations by deploying hybrid cables, which combine fiber (data) and copper (remote power) in one cable. Before Belden’s hybrid termination box was released, installers had no choice but to install fiber and copper in an enclosure that put exposed fiber at risk of damage when copper conductors were terminated in the same space. Because cables came to the enclosure from any direction, density and termination were also difficult to manage. The DuetConnect Hybrid Termination Box solves these problems, making hybrid cable termination easy, clean and efficient—all while separating copper and fiber for maximum protection and performance. Multiple cable entry points allow for installation flexibility, and each module can support up to four fibers and four copper conductors. Network managers can easily add density in the future by simply stacking one DuetConnect Hybrid Termination Box on top of another with up to three stackable boxes, making it faster and easier to juggle the challenges associated with rapid fiber-infrastructure expansion. “With the DuetConnect Hybrid Termination Box, installers can quickly and easily terminate and separate fiber and copper in a single box, saving time and space. Walls can even be used as conduits for hybrid cable by installing directly onto a junction box or in plenum spaces,” says Sandra Imrazene, fiber systems product manager at Belden. title: The true cost of Employee Disengagement in a Hybrid Workplace
summary: Learn why disengaged employees cost billions in lost productivity, undermining company culture and fostering high turnover rates; and how to invest in engagement.
body_text: In the fast-paced business world, where profit margins and quarterly reports dominate conversations, it's easy to lose sight of a company's most valuable asset: its employees. Any organization will claim that a strong team is its most valuable asset. Employees are the foundation of every business, setting its foundation for success. Investing in their workers becomes critical as CEOs attempt to lead their companies toward success. After all, firms that prioritize employee experience and culture have excellent retention rates and create a more lively work environment, whether hybrid or not. Corporations tend to see employees as data rather than what they bring to the table, which is a company's vitality. Employees are the foundation of every firm, setting the platform for success via creativity and productivity. As a result, traditional organizations treat employees as just numbers, and employee engagement plummets, with severe consequences for the company’s work culture. ‍ The post-pandemic and RTO area Take a step back four years and zoom out to a global scale. Understanding employee disengagement often begins with a moment of revelation, a realization that challenges our preconceived notions. The COVID-19 pandemic was a wake-up call, with the start of hybrid work prompting a deeper introspection into workplace satisfaction and productivity dynamics. "While employee engagement had been on the rise for the past decade, the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted this upward trajectory," observes Dr. Michael Wong, a leading economist specializing in labor markets. "Now, more than ever, companies must prioritize engagement initiatives to foster resilience and adaptability in the face of global challenges." Contrary to popular belief, employee engagement is not a default condition in which companies do not need to commit their time. While some firms thrive at it, many need to heighten their employee engagement. It's an outlier, not the standard. The average US workforce includes 16.2% actively disengaged employees. The economic implications are considerable, with billions of dollars wasted each year due to disengagement difficulties. ‍ Effects of Turnover Rates: This leads to dissatisfaction, lack of motivation, and a weak company culture, leading to a higher turnover rate. While cutting corners on employee satisfaction may seem to save money, the reality paints a different picture within work culture. High turnover rates are a common consequence of disengagement, which inflicts costs on organizations regarding recruitment expenses and lost productivity. The Center for American Progress reveals that the average turnover of an employee costs about one-third of the worker's salary. This figure can skyrocket to an alarming 200% for highly skilled, long-term employees. The costs associated with employee turnover extend far beyond the initial hiring process explains Dr. Sarah Johnson, a leading researcher in organizational psychology. From recruitment expenses to lost productivity during the transition period, the financial implications are staggering. Consider a scenario in the technology sector where the turnover rate is 13%. For a 1,000-person company, the cost of losing 130 employees annually is astronomical. Factoring in recruitment, training, development, and lost productivity expenses, the total expense balloons a staggering $6.5 million annually. ‍ ‍ The Financial Implications The economic impact of disengaged employees remains alarmingly consistent, and the financial implications of lost productivity alone are massive. Disengaged employees worldwide cost the economy $8.8 trillion in lost productivity, equivalent to 9% of global GDP . Overall, employee engagement has declined, with the number of actively engaged employees dropping by two percentage points since 2019 . This downward trajectory is concerning, as it predates the pandemic, especially considering remote work, signaling deeper systemic issues within organizations. To put these figures into perspective, let's consider a hypothetical scenario. Imagine a 200-person company in the Atlanta metro area with an average salary of $74,000 annually. Assuming that 17% of employees are actively disengaged, each costing 34% of their annual salary in disengagement costs, the yearly financial burden amounts to a staggering $855,440. However, this figure only scratches the surface of the actual cost of disengagement. Gallup's statistics predominantly focus on actively disengaged employees, neglecting the substantial portion categorized as "not engaged." Even a conservative estimate of the impact of this group underscores the magnitude of the challenge facing organizations. ‍ More than a Financial Loss " The negative impact of disengagement goes beyond financial losses," remarks Dr. Emily Che n, a renowned expert in organizational behavior. "A toxic work environment, characterized by low morale and diminished productivity, can erode company culture and drive talented employees away." While effective in attracting talent, financial incentives need to foster genuine engagement. While a competitive salary may make employees feel secure, there needs to be employee engagement, a sense of ownership, and passion about the company for sustained productivity. Otherwise, productivity takes a nosedive as disengaged employees contribute less, make more errors, and are prone to absenteeism. Disengaged employees cost U.S. companies $450 billion to $550 billion annually in lost productivity. Teams rating high on engagement metrics enjoy many benefits, including heightened customer loyalty, increased profitability, and enhanced productivity. Engaged work cultures outperform their peers and demonstrate resilience in economic downturns, underscoring the strategic significance of fostering a culture of engagement. Despite these statistics, companies can proactively combat employee disengagement and its associated costs. Investing in employee experience, cultivating a positive work culture, and offering competitive benefits boost engagement and retention rates. Strong leadership, coupled with a supportive work environment, lays the groundwork for employee engagement emphasizes Dr. Rachel Martinez, a seasoned HR consultant. "By prioritizing employee well-being and fostering a sense of belonging, companies can mitigate the financial losses incurred by disengagement." ‍ Furthermore, transparency and accountability are paramount in engaging employees, with leaders making changes based on input. Regular check-ins and pulse surveys enable organizations to gauge progress and adjust strategies accordingly, fostering a positive work culture of continuous improvement. Investing in employee engagement is not just a moral imperative; it's a sound business decision with tangible returns on investment. The costs of inaction far outweigh the resources required to cultivate a highly engaged workforce. Organizations can unlock untapped potential by prioritizing engagement, driving innovation, productivity, and sustainable success in today's competitive landscape. Conclusion As we continue to see companies transform in every way, leadership must take this opportunity to redefine the future of work. The road ahead may be fraught with challenges, but the rewards of a highly engaged workforce are undeniable. Together, let us embark on this adventure, armed with the knowledge that the value of employee engagement transcends mere economics—it's the cornerstone of organizational vitality and resilience in an ever-changing world. ‍

title: The History of Go Links®
summary: Go links have been around for almost a decade, but who invented the golink? Learn the history of go links and why this is such a great tool.
body_text: Internal short links (aka go links® ) have been around since the early 2000s and have matured and adapted drastically in the past 18 years, migrating their way into the tech industry. What is a go link®? It’s essentially a memorable short link that’s easy to type into your browser for instant access to any resource. In this article, we’ll give you a quick overview of the history of go links, including: Internal go links at Google Internal go links at NCSU Yo links at Yahoo The first SaaS version The first go links app Go links history timeline 2006: Internal go links at Google In 2006, Eric DeFriez and Benjamin Staffin worked together at Google and identified the need for a solution like go links®. They often received requests to create shortcut URLs, and to make things easier, they wanted to create an internal solution that all employees could use. Eric created a similar go link system, which brought in the use of the “go/” domain and enabled Googlers to easily access links by typing “go/link” in their browser. Benjamin compared this go links system to AOL keywords used on the corporate network. By the end of 2006, they had finished and launched the first internal go links application at Google. The app quickly became a key component of the Google ecosystem, with widespread use for sharing links within the company. 2010: Internal go links at NCSU In 2009, another internal version of go links was emerging at North Carolina State University. Nick Young , who worked in IT, wanted to make it easier for the student body to share resources in classrooms, posters, emails, social media, and more. Nick developed his own short link system and released the final version to NCSU on October 10, 2010. 2012: Yo links at Yahoo In 2012, when Marissa Mayer left Google to become the CEO of Yahoo, a similar go links application popped up at Yahoo, but with a twist: yo/links. From 2012 to 2015, as more people left Google to join other tech companies, they realized just how important a short link application was to completing everyday tasks. Soon the internal application started showing up all around Silicon Valley as engineers built similar systems at: Linkedin, Twitter, Square, Netflix, PayPal, Stripe, Airbnb, Optimizely, Mixpanel, Nextdoor, and more. 2016: The first SaaS version of go links In 2014, Jorge Zamora worked at Yahoo. As he began visiting friends at other tech companies in Silicon Valley, he noticed that they had the same thing: go/links. The links would be posted in the cafeterias, break rooms, and hallways; you couldn’t miss them. Each application was usually built by an engineer inside the company and served the simple purpose of redirecting URLs. Jorge saw that these applications could be improved significantly and made available to the public: GoLinks as a Service . So he reached out to some old college friends, started a team, and began working on his own GoLinks system. He wanted to create something that would be available to any company, not just tech giants. On August 29, 2016, he released the first SaaS version of GoLinks® . This application was more than just a basic redirect system. It could be set up for a whole company in a matter of minutes—no software installation needed. All you had to do was install the extension in any browser, and go links were there to use whenever you needed them. This tool empowered anyone, not just engineers, to easily implement a golinks system at their own company. With go link features like a Slack application, browser quick search, on-page creation, NLP suggestions for misspelled links, DNS public, and private entries, and Single Sign-On solutions, this would become the single choice for enterprise clients choosing a golinks solution . Since then, similar short link tools built by individuals have popped up here and there. These are usually open-source projects that involve a lot of setup, knowledge of installing applications, and limited support. 2022: The first go links® mobile app By 2022, GoLinks Inc. had grown to a mid-sized company with hundreds of customers like Asana, Moderna, Rokt, and Checkr using the product. With this momentum, they launched the first go link mobile application . Remote work changed how we work, and people aren’t just at their desks all day. This app allowed employees to securely access work resources, anytime and anywhere. Get started with go links There you have it—the full history of go links. If you’re interested in trying out this tool yourself, head to https://www.golinks.io/ and see why the go link is quickly becoming the most valuable productivity tool in Silicon Valley.
